title: AI Governance Risk Tiering for Sustainable Digital Infrastructure: A Systematic Review of Cybersecurity Frameworks
explain_beginner: AI is being used more and more in public services and important infrastructure, and that brings real risks to privacy and fairness that today's rules do not handle well. This paper reviewed 450 research records and closely studied 95 of them. The authors found that current AI governance is scattered: some frameworks focus on ethics and privacy, others on rules and risk, and few combine both. Their main contribution is a model that sorts AI risks into tiers and links each tier to concrete technical checks, turning broad principles into steps organizations can actually audit and follow.
explain_business: AI adoption across services and critical infrastructure is outpacing existing governance, which struggles with privacy, bias, transparency and accountability risks. This review of 95 studies shows the current landscape is fragmented, with most frameworks either ethics-focused or compliance-focused and few doing both. The practical takeaway is a risk-tiering matrix that connects principles to auditable technical controls, aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 9. For executives, this informs decisions about which governance model to adopt, how to prioritize controls by risk tier, and how to prepare for audits, supporting secure and sustainable AI deployment rather than one-off policy statements.
explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a systematic literature review following PRISMA 2020, screening 450 records from major databases and analyzing 95 high-quality studies. They applied principal component analysis and k-means clustering to map the governance landscape. Outputs include a heat map of frameworks, a theme co-occurrence network, a cluster analysis of framework coverage, and an integrated governance risk framework with a risk-tiering matrix. Results show a fragmented field split between ethics/privacy-centric and compliance/risk-focused approaches, with few integrated frameworks and tension between privacy and security. The matrix links ethical principles to auditable technical controls, addressing the translation step most frameworks omit.
